claim: Two calcified nodules were discovered among a woman's remains at the base of the ribs during excavations of a Late Byzantine era cemetery at Troy, Anatolia.
source: During excavations of a Late Byzantine era cemetery at the periphery of the ancient city of Troy, Anatolia (in present day Turkey) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we discovered two calcified nodules among a woman's remains.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript describing the discovery of the nodules.

claim: The nodules are 2–3 cm in diameter and composed of concentric layers.
source: The nodules, which are 2–3 cm in diameter and composed of concentric layers (Figure 1B), were discovered at the base of the ribs.
evidence: Direct measurement and observation reported in text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The woman was estimated to be 30 (±5y) at the time of death.
source: The woman was estimated to be 30 (±5y) at the time of death (Appendix).
evidence: Age estimation reported with reference to Appendix.

claim: Radiocarbon dating of the decedent's ulna yielded 790-860y BP.
source: Radiocarbon dating of the decedent's ulna yielded 790-860y BP (Supplementary file 1A), in agreement with the archeological assessment of the age of the cemetery (early 13th century AD, Appendix).
evidence: Direct radiocarbon dating results reported with reference to supplementary data.

claim: The radiocarbon date is in agreement with the archeological assessment of the cemetery as early 13th century AD.
source: Radiocarbon dating of the decedent's ulna yielded 790-860y BP (Supplementary file 1A), in agreement with the archeological assessment of the age of the cemetery (early 13th century AD, Appendix).
evidence: Comparison between radiocarbon dating and archaeological assessment.

claim: Nodule one is primarily composed of hydroxylapatite (bioapatite) and whitlockite, both of which have been found in human calcified pathological concretions.
source: Nodule one (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1B) is primarily composed of two phosphate phases, hydroxylapatite (bioapatite) and whitlockite (as well as small amounts of calcite), both of which have been found in human calcified pathological concretions (Lagier and Baud, 2003).
evidence: XRD analysis results with citation to prior literature on these minerals in pathological concretions.

claim: Struvite and calcium oxalate, common constituents of urinary stones, were absent in both XRD and SEM-EDS analyses.
source: However, struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) and calcium oxalate, common constituents of urinary stones, were absent in both XRD and SEM-EDS analyses (Supplementary file 1B-D).
evidence: Negative findings from XRD and SEM-EDS analyses.

claim: SEM of the nodules revealed aggregates of spherical structures with dimensions typical of bacterial cells.
source: SEM of the nodules (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) revealed aggregates of spherical structures with dimensions typical of bacterial cells, as well as extracellular polymeric substances (EPS – a glycocalyx secreted by the cells during biofilm formation [Decho and Thiel, 2011]).
evidence: SEM imaging results showing bacterial-sized structures.

claim: SEM of the nodules revealed extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), a glycocalyx secreted by cells during biofilm formation.
source: SEM of the nodules (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) revealed aggregates of spherical structures with dimensions typical of bacterial cells, as well as extracellular polymeric substances (EPS – a glycocalyx secreted by the cells during biofilm formation [Decho and Thiel, 2011]).
evidence: SEM imaging results with citation to literature on EPS and biofilm formation.

claim: Shotgun sequences from all libraries yielded 24–48% human, 37–66% S. saprophyticus, and 5–7% G. vaginalis DNA.
source: Shotgun sequences from all libraries yielded astonishingly high proportions of endogenous human and bacterial DNA: 24–48% human, 37–66% S. saprophyticus, and 5–7% G. vaginalis (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–5).
evidence: Metagenomic sequencing results showing DNA composition.

claim: A human mitochondrial genome was reconstructed at 30.1x unique read depth.
source: From these data, we reconstructed a human mitochondrial genome at 30.1x unique read depth, the consensus of which belongs to haplotype U3b3.
evidence: Genome reconstruction results with coverage depth reported.

claim: The consensus mitochondrial genome belongs to haplotype U3b3.
source: From these data, we reconstructed a human mitochondrial genome at 30.1x unique read depth, the consensus of which belongs to haplotype U3b3.
evidence: Haplogroup assignment from mitochondrial genome sequence.

claim: In phylogenetic analyses, the Troy mitogenome groups most closely with those from the Caucasus and Middle East.
source: In phylogenetic analyses of the mitogenome from Troy and modern mitogenomes, the Troy sample groups most closely with those from the Caucasus and Middle East, both of which were within the eastern limits of Late Byzantine influence (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis results showing geographic clustering.

claim: The Caucasus and Middle East were within the eastern limits of Late Byzantine influence.
source: In phylogenetic analyses of the mitogenome from Troy and modern mitogenomes, the Troy sample groups most closely with those from the Caucasus and Middle East, both of which were within the eastern limits of Late Byzantine influence (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Historical context provided in the manuscript.

claim: The mitochondrial genome from the ulna was reconstructed to an average unique coverage depth of 30.8x.
source: To investigate whether the nodules belonged to the associated female individual, we extracted DNA from her ulna, constructed a dsDNA library, enriched for, sequenced, and reconstructed the mitogenome to an average unique coverage depth of 30.8x.
evidence: Genome reconstruction results with coverage depth reported.

claim: The nodule and the ulna share the identical mitochondrial haplotype.
source: The nodule and the ulna share the identical mitochondrial haplotype (Supplementary file 1E), indicating that they stem from the same individual or a maternal relative.
evidence: Comparison of mitochondrial haplotypes from two samples.

claim: The identical mitochondrial haplotype indicates that the nodule and ulna stem from the same individual or a maternal relative.
source: The nodule and the ulna share the identical mitochondrial haplotype (Supplementary file 1E), indicating that they stem from the same individual or a maternal relative.
evidence: Inference based on mitochondrial DNA inheritance patterns.

claim: The metagenomic profile of the nodules suggests they derive from an amalgam of human and bacterial cells, as in an abscess.
source: The metagenomic profile of the nodules suggests they derive from an amalgam of human and bacterial cells, as in an abscess.
evidence: Interpretation of metagenomic data.

claim: The high concentration of S. saprophyticus and G. vaginalis DNA suggests an origin in genitourinary tissue.
source: The high concentration of S. saprophyticus and G. vaginalis DNA suggests an origin in genitourinary tissue.
evidence: Inference based on bacterial species typically associated with genitourinary tract.

claim: The similarity in abundance of G. vaginalis in the nodules and modern HMP vaginal samples points to a likely origin for the nodules in the female reproductive tract.
source: The similarity in abundance of G. vaginalis in the nodules and modern Human Microbiome Panel (HMP) vaginal samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 7) points to a likely origin for the nodules in the female reproductive tract.
evidence: Comparison with modern microbiome data from known anatomical sites.

claim: The metagenomic profile of the nodules (minus their associated blanks) is distinct from the sediment.
source: The metagenomic profile of the nodules (minus their associated blanks) is distinct from the sediment, whereas the reads from the ulna group closely with the sediment sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: PCA analysis showing separation of samples.

claim: The reads from the ulna group closely with the sediment sample.
source: The metagenomic profile of the nodules (minus their associated blanks) is distinct from the sediment, whereas the reads from the ulna group closely with the sediment sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: PCA analysis showing clustering of samples.

claim: The nodules were less prone to leaching of environmental DNA compared to the ulna.
source: These results indicate that the nodules were less prone to leaching of environmental DNA.
evidence: Inference from metagenomic profile differences between nodules and ulna.

claim: Bacterial and inflammatory cells were replicated in calcium phosphate minerals ('ghost cells').
source: Our SEM-EDS and XRD findings suggest that bacterial and inflammatory cells were replicated in calcium phosphate minerals ('ghost cells'); it is likely that this mineralization provided a remarkable degree of protection from DNA degradation and environmental leaching as seen in the bones.
evidence: Interpretation of SEM-EDS and XRD findings.

claim: Mineralization of the nodules provided a remarkable degree of protection from DNA degradation and environmental leaching.
source: Our SEM-EDS and XRD findings suggest that bacterial and inflammatory cells were replicated in calcium phosphate minerals ('ghost cells'); it is likely that this mineralization provided a remarkable degree of protection from DNA degradation and environmental leaching as seen in the bones.
evidence: Inference based on DNA preservation differences between nodules and bone.

claim: The ectopic, inflammation-related calcification observed is an apparently highly effective mechanism of bacterial fossilization that rivals mineralization occurring at much slower rates in the environment.
source: The ectopic, inflammation-related calcification observed here is an apparently highly effective mechanism of bacterial fossilization that rivals mineralization occurring at much slower rates in the environment.
evidence: Interpretation of DNA preservation quality in calcified nodules.

claim: Sexing analyses of the nodules assign them as female -XX.
source: Sexing analyses of the remains (and associated blanks) using the method of Skoglund et al. (2013) assign the nodules as female -XX (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: Sex determination from DNA using established method.

claim: Shotgun sequencing data from the nodules contained 884 reads conservatively mapping to the Y chromosome.
source: More thorough analyses of the human DNA present in the nodules yielded an intriguing finding that helps pinpoint their tissue of origin. Shotgun sequencing data from the nodules contained a small number of reads (884) conservatively mapping to the Y chromosome (Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: Direct sequencing results showing Y chromosome reads.

claim: The length distributions of Y chromosome reads overlapped with those mapping to the X chromosome and autosomes, suggesting an endogenous, ancient origin.
source: The length distributions of the reads overlapped with those mapping to the X chromosome and autosomes, suggesting an endogenous, ancient origin (Supplementary file 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 5); we searched for but did not find similar bona fide ancient Y chromosome reads in sequence data from the ulna, the sediment, or any negative control (Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: Fragment length analysis consistent with ancient DNA characteristics.

claim: No similar bona fide ancient Y chromosome reads were found in sequence data from the ulna, the sediment, or any negative control.
source: The length distributions of the reads overlapped with those mapping to the X chromosome and autosomes, suggesting an endogenous, ancient origin (Supplementary file 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 5); we searched for but did not find similar bona fide ancient Y chromosome reads in sequence data from the ulna, the sediment, or any negative control (Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: Negative control results supporting authenticity of Y chromosome reads in nodules.

claim: The presence of Y chromosome reads in the nodule but not in the ulna could be explained by a placental origin of the mineralized abscesses, indicating chorioamnionitis in the decedent while pregnant with a male fetus.
source: The presence of Y chromosome reads in the nodule but not in the ulna could be explained by a placental origin of the mineralized abscesses, indicating chorioamnionitis in the decedent while pregnant with a male fetus.
evidence: Inference based on presence of male DNA in female tissue.

claim: Chorioamnionitis involves an inflammatory response on the part of the fetus as well as the mother, which would explain a female (maternal) origin of the nodular tissue with a minority male (fetal) component.
source: Chorioamnionitis – inflammation and infection of the placenta and fetal membranes – involves an inflammatory response on the part of the fetus as well as the mother (Kraus et al., 2004), which would explain a female (maternal) origin of the nodular tissue with a minority male (fetal) component.
evidence: Explanation based on known pathophysiology of chorioamnionitis with citation.

claim: Chorioamnionitis is a mixed infection in which vaginal bacteria reach the upper reproductive tract, placenta, and fetal membranes.
source: Chorioamnionitis is a mixed infection in which vaginal bacteria reach the upper reproductive tract, placenta, and fetal membranes; G. vaginalis is often identified in infected tissues (Hillier et al., 1988).
evidence: Definition and characteristics of chorioamnionitis with citation.

claim: G. vaginalis is often identified in chorioamnionitis infected tissues.
source: Chorioamnionitis is a mixed infection in which vaginal bacteria reach the upper reproductive tract, placenta, and fetal membranes; G. vaginalis is often identified in infected tissues (Hillier et al., 1988).
evidence: Citation to prior literature on G. vaginalis in chorioamnionitis.

claim: S. saprophyticus can be found among the genitourinary and gastrointestinal flora of healthy women.
source: S. saprophyticus can be found among the genitourinary and gastrointestinal flora of healthy women (Ringertz and Torssander, 1986; Rupp et al., 1992; Schneider and Riley, 1996).
evidence: Citations to prior literature on S. saprophyticus colonization.

claim: S. saprophyticus is a common cause of urinary tract infection (UTI) in reproductive aged women.
source: It is a common cause of urinary tract infection (UTI) in reproductive aged women (Kahlmeter, 2003) and has also been known to cause puerperal infections (Arianpour et al., 2009).
evidence: Citation to prior literature on S. saprophyticus as UTI pathogen.

claim: S. saprophyticus has been known to cause puerperal infections.
source: It is a common cause of urinary tract infection (UTI) in reproductive aged women (Kahlmeter, 2003) and has also been known to cause puerperal infections (Arianpour et al., 2009).
evidence: Citation to prior literature on S. saprophyticus causing puerperal infections.

claim: A nearly complete genome of S. saprophyticus Troy was reconstructed, including >100 Kb of novel sequence compared to reference strain ATCC 15305.
source: We used a combination of paired-end reference guided assembly and iterative assembly to reconstruct a nearly complete genome of S. saprophyticus Troy, including >100 Kb of novel sequence compared to reference strain ATCC 15305.
evidence: Genome assembly results with comparison to reference.

claim: The S. saprophyticus Troy genome is 2,471,881 bp long, with an average unique coverage depth of 298.6x.
source: The genome is 2,471,881 bp long, with an average unique coverage depth of 298.6x (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), which represents an unprecedented, detailed and complete picture of an ancient pathogen genome from shotgun sequencing data.
evidence: Genome assembly statistics.

claim: The S. saprophyticus Troy genome represents an unprecedented, detailed and complete picture of an ancient pathogen genome from shotgun sequencing data.
source: The genome is 2,471,881 bp long, with an average unique coverage depth of 298.6x (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), which represents an unprecedented, detailed and complete picture of an ancient pathogen genome from shotgun sequencing data.
evidence: Claim about the quality and completeness of the ancient genome.

claim: A 22.6 Kb plasmid, pSST1, was reconstructed from S. saprophyticus Troy.
source: We also reconstructed a 22.6 Kb plasmid, pSST1.
evidence: Plasmid assembly result.

claim: A contiguous G. vaginalis genome could not be reconstructed due to high variability in coverage and lack of synteny in both ancient and modern genomic data.
source: We were unable to reconstruct a contiguous G. vaginalis genome due to high variability in coverage and lack of synteny in both ancient and modern genomic data (Ahmed et al., 2012).
evidence: Explanation of assembly limitations with citation to prior work showing similar issues.

claim: 1187 unique contigs (total length 1,435,761 bp) corresponding to 972 annotated genes were recovered from G. vaginalis Troy with an average unique coverage depth of 57.0x.
source: Using this method, we recovered 1187 unique contigs (total length 1,435,761 bp) corresponding to 972 annotated genes and an average unique coverage depth of 57.0x (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: De novo assembly statistics for G. vaginalis.

claim: The sample of 35 isolates of G. vaginalis was grouped into four previously defined clades.
source: Our sample of 35 isolates of G. vaginalis was grouped into four previously defined clades (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4), which have been proposed to represent distinct species (Ahmed et al., 2012).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis results with reference to prior clade definitions.

claim: The four G. vaginalis clades have been proposed to represent distinct species.
source: Our sample of 35 isolates of G. vaginalis was grouped into four previously defined clades (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4), which have been proposed to represent distinct species (Ahmed et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation to prior literature proposing species-level distinctions.

claim: G. vaginalis Troy sits within Clade 1, among vaginal and endometrial isolates collected from both healthy women and patients with bacterial vaginosis.
source: G. vaginalis Troy sits within Clade 1, among vaginal and endometrial isolates collected from both healthy women and patients with bacterial vaginosis.
evidence: Phylogenetic placement of ancient strain among modern isolates.

claim: The 800-year-old G. vaginalis sample from Troy falls within contemporary genetic diversity.
source: Interestingly, the 800-year-old sample from Troy (Turkey) falls within contemporary genetic diversity (Supplementary file 1I).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis showing ancient strain nested within modern diversity.

claim: Extensive impacts of lateral gene transfer (LGT) were identified on G. vaginalis diversity.
source: Consistent with prior reports (Ahmed et al., 2012), we identified extensive impacts of lateral gene transfer (LGT) on G. vaginalis diversity (Figure 3).
evidence: Recombination analysis results with citation to prior work.

claim: In the G. vaginalis core genome alignment, which contains just 44% of per-isolate gene content, 20% of sites have been affected by recombination.
source: Even in the core genome alignment, which contains just 44% of per-isolate gene content, we estimate that 20% of sites have been affected by recombination.
evidence: Quantitative recombination analysis results.

claim: The high rate of recombination in G. vaginalis may help to explain the remarkable preservation of genetic diversity.
source: This high rate of recombination may help to explain the remarkable preservation of genetic diversity in G. vaginalis.
evidence: Inference connecting recombination rate to diversity preservation.

claim: A recent study of Helicobacter pylori, which has similarly high rates of LGT, found that genetic diversity within the species has been preserved for more than five thousand years.
source: A recent study of Helicobacter pylori, which has similarly high rates of LGT, found that genetic diversity within the species has been preserved for more than five thousand years (Maixner et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to prior study on another species with high recombination.

claim: Two distinct clades of S. saprophyticus were discovered.
source: We discovered two distinct clades of S. saprophyticus (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), one of which (Clade P) appears to be more strongly associated with pathogenicity and includes our ancient S. saprophyticus Troy.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis identifying two major clades.

claim: Clade P appears to be more strongly associated with pathogenicity and includes S. saprophyticus Troy.
source: We discovered two distinct clades of S. saprophyticus (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), one of which (Clade P) appears to be more strongly associated with pathogenicity and includes our ancient S. saprophyticus Troy.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis with association to clinical phenotype.

claim: Nineteen of twenty veterinary and human clinical isolates belong to Clade P, an association that was statistically significant.
source: Nineteen of twenty veterinary and human clinical isolates belong to Clade P, an association that was statistically significant (Appendix).
evidence: Statistical analysis of clade-phenotype association.

claim: Clade E is made up of food and environmental isolates of S. saprophyticus, as well as a human UTI isolate from Japan.
source: A second clade (Clade E) is made up of food and environmental isolates of S. saprophyticus, as well as a human UTI isolate from Japan.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis showing composition of Clade E.

claim: The human clinical isolates in Clades P and E are nested within the phylogeny with more divergent lineages associated with other animals.
source: The human clinical isolates in Clades P and E are nested within the phylogeny with more divergent lineages associated with other animals.
evidence: Phylogenetic tree topology showing relationship between human and animal isolates.

claim: The phylogeny suggests that the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of S. saprophyticus may not have been human-associated.
source: This suggests that the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of S. saprophyticus may not have been human-associated.
evidence: Inference from phylogenetic tree structure.

claim: This is in stark contrast to Staphylococcus aureus, where phylogenetic studies suggest that the MRCA of human and livestock-associated lineages had a human host.
source: This is in stark contrast to the major pathogen in the genus, Staphylococcus aureus, where phylogenetic studies suggest that the MRCA of human and livestock-associated lineages had a human host (Fitzgerald, 2012; Weinert et al., 2012; Shepheard et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison to prior phylogenetic studies of S. aureus with citations.

claim: S. aureus is strongly associated with its niche on the human body and is transmitted primarily from person-to-person.
source: S. aureus is strongly associated with its niche on the human body and is transmitted primarily from person-to-person.
evidence: Statement about S. aureus ecology based on established knowledge.

claim: S. saprophyticus appears to be a generalist that colonizes a range of environments.
source: S. saprophyticus, by contrast, appears to be a generalist that colonizes a range of environments.
evidence: Inference from phylogenetic and ecological data.

claim: In northern climates, there is marked seasonal variation in the incidence of S. saprophyticus UTI.
source: In northern climates, there is marked seasonal variation in the incidence of S. saprophyticus UTI (Rupp et al., 1992; Hovelius and Mårdh, 1984; Ringertz and Torssander, 1986; Hedman et al., 1993; Widerström et al., 2007), whereas there is no evidence of seasonality in Mediterranean climates (Schneider and Riley, 1996).
evidence: Citations to multiple prior epidemiological studies.

claim: There is no evidence of seasonality in S. saprophyticus UTI in Mediterranean climates.
source: In northern climates, there is marked seasonal variation in the incidence of S. saprophyticus UTI (Rupp et al., 1992; Hovelius and Mårdh, 1984; Ringertz and Torssander, 1986; Hedman et al., 1993; Widerström et al., 2007), whereas there is no evidence of seasonality in Mediterranean climates (Schneider and Riley, 1996).
evidence: Citation to prior epidemiological study.

claim: S. saprophyticus can be identified in environmental samples, with a strong seasonal peak that occurs just before peak rates of S. saprophyticus UTI in northern climates.
source: S. saprophyticus can be identified in environmental samples, with a strong seasonal peak that occurs just before peak rates of S. saprophyticus UTI in northern climates (Hedman et al., 1993; Soge et al., 2009).
evidence: Citations to prior environmental sampling studies.

claim: Molecular epidemiological surveys suggest S. saprophyticus is primarily acquired from an environmental reservoir, rather than as a result of person-to-person transmission.
source: Molecular epidemiological surveys also suggest S. saprophyticus is primarily acquired from an environmental reservoir, rather than as a result of person-to-person transmission (Widerström et al., 2007; Widerström et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations to prior molecular epidemiology studies.

claim: The observations suggest that S. saprophyticus bacteria cycle between host-associated and environmental stages, with seasonal climatic effects on their abundance in the environment.
source: These observations suggest that the bacteria cycle between host-associated and environmental stages, with seasonal climatic effects on their abundance in the environment.
evidence: Inference from multiple lines of epidemiological evidence.

claim: The length of the branch leading to S. saprophyticus Troy is similar to those leading to the other tips, suggesting there is little temporal signal in the phylogeny.
source: The length of the branch leading to S. saprophyticus Troy is similar to those leading to the other tips (Figure 4A), suggesting there is little temporal signal in the phylogeny.
evidence: Observation from phylogenetic tree branch lengths.

claim: Calibrated phylogenetic analyses confirmed the absence of temporal signal, which precludes reliable estimation of the rate of substitution or divergence times for S. saprophyticus.
source: Calibrated phylogenetic analyses (Appendix) confirmed the absence of temporal signal, which precludes reliable estimation of the rate of substitution or divergence times for S. saprophyticus.
evidence: Results from molecular clock analysis.

claim: A mixed environmental, commensal and pathogenic niche may in part explain the absence of temporal structure in the sample of S. saprophyticus.
source: A mixed environmental, commensal and pathogenic niche may in part explain the absence of temporal structure in our sample of S. saprophyticus.
evidence: Speculation about causes of lack of temporal signal.

claim: Selection pressures and generation times are likely to differ between free-living and host-associated stages, which can obscure temporal signals in genetic data.
source: Selection pressures and generation times are likely to differ between free-living and host-associated stages, which can obscure temporal signals in genetic data (Bromham, 2009).
evidence: Explanation with citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: Periods of dormancy in the environment would be predicted to lower the overall rate at which S. saprophyticus evolves.
source: In addition to producing rate variability, periods of dormancy in the environment – e.g. during the winter in northern climates, as suggested by seasonal patterns in cultivability – would be predicted to lower the overall rate at which S. saprophyticus evolves (Bromham, 2009; Weinert et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on theoretical considerations with citations.

claim: The 800 year interval between S. saprophyticus Troy and the other tips may be too short relative to the overall depth of the tree to allow reliable rate inference.
source: The 800 year interval between S. saprophyticus Troy and the other tips may simply be too short relative to the overall depth of the tree to allow reliable rate inference.
evidence: Speculation about temporal sampling limitations.

claim: All human-associated isolates of S. saprophyticus in Clade P form a monophyletic group, to which the bovine mastitis strain falls basally.
source: Notably, all human-associated isolates of S. saprophyticus in Clade P form a monophyletic group, to which the bovine mastitis strain falls basally; there are no modern human pathogenic representatives of the S. saprophyticus Troy lineage.
evidence: Observation from phylogenetic tree topology.

claim: There are no modern human pathogenic representatives of the S. saprophyticus Troy lineage.
source: Notably, all human-associated isolates of S. saprophyticus in Clade P form a monophyletic group, to which the bovine mastitis strain falls basally; there are no modern human pathogenic representatives of the S. saprophyticus Troy lineage.
evidence: Observation from phylogenetic analysis and sample composition.

claim: The ecology of S. saprophyticus may have differed in the Byzantine world, with human infections arising from a different reservoir of bacteria than they do today.
source: This may mean that the ecology of S. saprophyticus differed in the Byzantine world, with human infections arising from a different reservoir of bacteria than they do today.
evidence: Speculation based on phylogenetic placement of ancient strain.

claim: S. saprophyticus is readily cultured from the environment around livestock.
source: S. saprophyticus is readily cultured from the environment around livestock (Hedman et al., 1993; Cherif-Antar et al., 2016), and Byzantine era peasants in Anatolia typically shared their households with cattle (Lefort, 2007).
evidence: Citations to prior environmental sampling studies.

claim: Byzantine era peasants in Anatolia typically shared their households with cattle.
source: S. saprophyticus is readily cultured from the environment around livestock (Hedman et al., 1993; Cherif-Antar et al., 2016), and Byzantine era peasants in Anatolia typically shared their households with cattle (Lefort, 2007).
evidence: Citation to historical source on Byzantine living conditions.

claim: Historical settings with close human-livestock contact are likely to have facilitated spillover events and circulation of bacteria adapted to both livestock and humans.
source: This and other historical settings are likely to have facilitated spillover events and, perhaps, the circulation of bacteria that were adapted to both livestock and humans.
evidence: Speculation based on historical context and phylogenetic findings.

claim: It is not possible to determine whether the human clinical isolate nested among environmental and food-associated bacteria in Clade E represents a spillover or a second emergence into humans.
source: Based on the available data, it is not possible to determine whether the human clinical isolate nested among environmental and food-associated bacteria in Clade E represents a spillover or a second emergence into humans.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitation in interpreting phylogenetic data.

claim: S. saprophyticus can transition to a human pathogenic niche with relative ease.
source: In either event, it appears that S. saprophyticus can transition to a human pathogenic niche with relative ease.
evidence: Inference from phylogenetic evidence of multiple human-associated lineages.

claim: No gene content was identified as uniquely shared (or absent) among the pathogenic strains in the sample.
source: We did not identify any gene content uniquely shared (or absent) among the pathogenic strains in our sample, which suggests that pleiotropy underlies S. saprophyticus' flexible association with diverse niches.
evidence: Negative result from comparative genomics analysis.

claim: Pleiotropy underlies S. saprophyticus' flexible association with diverse niches.
source: We did not identify any gene content uniquely shared (or absent) among the pathogenic strains in our sample, which suggests that pleiotropy underlies S. saprophyticus' flexible association with diverse niches.
evidence: Inference from lack of pathogen-specific genes.

claim: For many bacterial genera, genetic distances between free-living organisms and pathogens are larger than observed in S. saprophyticus, and pathogen emergence is a singular event characterized by genomic decay and loss of functions required outside the pathogenic niche.
source: For many bacterial genera, genetic distances between free-living organisms and pathogens are larger than observed here, and pathogen emergence is a singular event characterized by genomic decay and loss of functions required outside the pathogenic niche (Parkhill et al., 2001; Larsson et al., 2009; Reuter et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison to prior studies of pathogen evolution with citations.

claim: The observations reinforce the notion that the adaptive paths to bacterial virulence are more diverse than has previously been appreciated.
source: More studies and wider sampling are needed to fully characterize the niche of S. saprophyticus, but our observations reinforce the notion that the adaptive paths to bacterial virulence are more diverse than has previously been appreciated.
evidence: Interpretation of findings in broader context of bacterial pathogen evolution.

claim: Complications of pregnancy and childbirth are major causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide and new threats to maternal health continue to emerge.
source: Complications of pregnancy and childbirth are major causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide and new threats to maternal health continue to emerge (WHO et al., 2014; Mlakar et al., 2016).
evidence: Citations to WHO report and recent literature on maternal health threats.

claim: The infection in the woman from Troy was associated with exuberant calcification of the placenta, which replicated maternal, fetal, and bacterial cells in calcium phosphate minerals.
source: Her infection was associated with exuberant calcification of the placenta, which replicated maternal, fetal, and bacterial cells in calcium phosphate minerals and preserved a high resolution molecular portrait of their contents.
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple analyses.

claim: S. saprophyticus Troy belongs to a lineage that appears to be uncommonly associated with human disease in the modern world.
source: S. saprophyticus Troy belongs to a lineage that appears to be uncommonly associated with human disease in the modern world, whereas G. vaginalis Troy nests among modern commensal and pathogenic strains on its phylogeny.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis showing ancient strain's relationship to modern isolates.

claim: G. vaginalis Troy nests among modern commensal and pathogenic strains on its phylogeny.
source: S. saprophyticus Troy belongs to a lineage that appears to be uncommonly associated with human disease in the modern world, whereas G. vaginalis Troy nests among modern commensal and pathogenic strains on its phylogeny.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis showing ancient strain's relationship to modern isolates.

claim: The findings highlight the complexity of virulence as a bacterial trait and a potential role of interactions among bacterial species in shaping pathologic outcomes of infection.
source: This highlights the complexity of virulence as a bacterial trait and a potential role of interactions among bacterial species in shaping pathologic outcomes of infection.
evidence: Interpretation of findings regarding mixed infection and virulence.

claim: Pregnancy complications are poorly represented in the archeological record, despite their importance in contemporary and ancient societies.
source: Pregnancy complications are poorly represented in the archeological record, despite their importance in contemporary and ancient societies.
evidence: Statement about archaeological record and importance of pregnancy complications.

claim: Scanning electron microscopy of the tissue revealed 'ghost cells', resulting from dystrophic calcification.
source: Scanning electron microscopy of the tissue revealed 'ghost cells', resulting from dystrophic calcification, which preserved ancient maternal, fetal and bacterial DNA of a severe infection, likely chorioamnionitis.
evidence: SEM findings with interpretation of calcification type.

claim: Ghost cells preserved ancient maternal, fetal and bacterial DNA of a severe infection, likely chorioamnionitis.
source: Scanning electron microscopy of the tissue revealed 'ghost cells', resulting from dystrophic calcification, which preserved ancient maternal, fetal and bacterial DNA of a severe infection, likely chorioamnionitis.
evidence: Integration of multiple lines of evidence to diagnose likely infection type.
